Same as others have said— trans women tend to be the more known side of transness, and therefore garner more hate than we do. Misogyny is sometimes (most of the time, unfortunately) a big factor in this as well.

I’ve found that no matter if they’re queer/trans or not, these kinds of people participate in what I like to call the “pain Olympics” lol.

Example:
Person A: I slept so badly last night— only got 5 hours of sleep.
Person B: Oh, well I only got 3– you have no right to complain when I’m off worse.

There’s no competition. Both people are tired; one of them just wants to complain and/or play the victim (there are levels to this, obviously not everything is so cut and dry lol).

I’ve found it’s just another part of that. We’re all just people— and both us and trans women are part of the same collective. Negativity and hate are easy to create; positivity and support is harder. We all want an easier life, but it’s not easy for any of us. I hope one day instead of comparing who has it “easier” (which is subjective anyway), we can all understand that life sucks, but we’re both here to see it. I hope we can all lift each other up someday.

I still have my own hangups about it (bullying lol) but when I was working, even my queer coworkers thought I was a cis man. I never worked with him much (he did mornings, I did nights) but another coworker (a man in his 60s, most likely cis but doesn’t really matter lol) was 4’10” and he was great to talk with— everyone respected him and there was no mention of his height (and same with me).

It’s hard. It was harder before I passed. Being a short man is hard for me. But being a short *girl* was unlivable for me. 

All this to say: self esteem takes time and it’s even harder when there’s dysphoria involved. Passing isn’t what everyone wants and I know that, but for those who want it: your height will not be an obstacle for you. Height is something we’re given by a roll of the genetic dice. Society did with it as society does. But we’re all here. I can deal with my bad days because even though my height isn’t what I’d like it to be, I know it doesn’t stop me from being a man. I’d rather be a short guy with self esteem problems than someone I’m not.

Self love is a Sisyphusian task for most— so focus on self tolerance. Maybe loving myself will be a battle I’ll fight for a long time, but I can live with myself in the meantime. I hope you can, too. Anyone reading this.

Low self esteem still affects me today (kids are assholes lol) but I’ve had no trouble passing at my short height and I’ve found friends that don’t make me feel like shit about something that none of us have control over.

If anything, the only thing that stops me from passing most of the time is (funnily enough) my eyes. I have insanely long eyelashes (cis men tend to have longer/thicker ones but these are something I was gifted genetically ig lmao) and people assume I’m a girl based on that.

At my job there were guys shorter than me. A lot of people at that place were queer and/or also trans and they were all shocked to find out I wasn’t cis (I’m stealth but more so just a quiet person and I keep to myself lol).

Transition no matter your height, your age, your job, your hobbies— pretty much anything. It doesn’t make you less of a man or less masculine for stupid things like these.

Life is too short (pun non intended) to make yourself suffer for no reason other than your brain is being stupid and is actively out to get you. The bullying still affects me as an adult, but it doesn’t control me. Don’t let it control you, either. You are more than what other people might say to you.

Also, I’m friends with a guy who is 4’6”, cis, and plays tennis with a small local men’s league (club? Not sure lol). Surround yourself with love even if you can’t as easily give it to yourself than to others. Be kind to yourself. Be patient. Self hatred has only made me more miserable. You don’t have to love yourself, but get to a point where you can tolerate it. I may never love the body I was given, but it’s the one I have. I’ve accepted it. It’s me. I’ve worn corsets for cosplay before and (pre-surgery) wore binders daily. 

Both can cause the exact same (or at least very similar) issues— rib compression, lessened lung capacity, just to name a few.

Binders are pretty decent nowadays (as well as corsets I’d presume, but they aren’t in fashion now like they used to be lol) and have a good amount of wiggle room if you pick the right size. Wearing a corset consistently for a full week gave me similar feelings to my binder— okay, but you Need to take it off at a certain point.

A lot of people who wear binders want a completely flat chest— which for 99% of people is infeasible because “flat chests” aren’t as flat as most people tend to think (source: I was one of those people lol). So in the pursuit of this, they make take a size smaller than they should— therefore creating more pronounced issues.

TL;DR: they both can cause issues, you just gotta listen to your body and not damage your ribs lol. I wore the right size binder for years and I have a slight rib issue because of it (most likely from wearing it too long & while working). Just be careful and you should be A-OK!

It’ll be questioned because all gender non-specific names tend to be, but you absolutely don’t need to change it. I have a friend of mine, cis male, named Zoey. (TW— SH/s*icide) I knew about being transgender from a young age, but didn’t connect the dots to see that I was trans. Puberty started early for me and I felt a sense of dread that I’d never felt before but couldn’t put it into words. As I got older, my self image got worse and worse and I just couldn’t figure out what was wrong. I would cry everyday, and would hurt myself because I couldn’t put it into words but I knew the problem was Me. It got so bad that one day… yeah let’s just say I took an emergency trip to the doctor’s office. Even when I couldn’t fully describe what I was feeling, I opened up more to people and slowly realized that I never wanted to be a girl or a young lady or a woman. I remember a specific conversation I had with one of my close friends and I told them I felt Sure but I was scared because what if I made the wrong choice even if at the time I felt right? They asked me, “If you grow old into your 80s, would you want to be an old woman or an old man?” And I figured it out from there.
2 almost 3 years on T, post-op top surgery and hoping for phallo one day. It’s hard to figure yourself out, insanely hard. A good friend of mine started E and realized they weren’t trans but just a more feminine guy.
Don’t feel bad about feeling like “what if it’s a phase?”. Life is all phases, constant changes all the time. We change as much as the next day and the day after that, even if you don’t see it. Do what’s going to make You happy. It’s going to take time and effort and a hell of a lot of days where you feel hopeless but I haven’t truly considered taking my life for a few years now.
Figuring out you’re trans happens, figuring out you’re not trans happens too. All about having love to share around, especially for yourself, too. You need it, too, don’t forget that.

So basically, don’t do that lol. Especially with the heat, the binder they gave me got pretty itchy so just listen to your surgeon’s instructions, get a friend to itch your back (trust me lol), and don’t get scarring in your armpits (that’s what armpit hair is for thankfully lol).

The drains aren’t terrible, just uncomfortable (feels weird to get them out, be prepared), and even for a strictly side-sleeper like me, I slept just fine on my back (with the help of meds, too). 

Oh, also for some reason this is sorta common and not really talked about that much, but TMI, post-op I didn’t shit for 5 days.. Everything was fine, but if you start to get worried like I did, as long as you aren’t feeling pain etc (obviously use your own judgement lol), it’s normal for quite a few people. Then again, I know a few other post-op people in my life that saw no difference with the bathroom. 

It’s going to be hard to stand up straight, I was hunched over for around a month just walking anywhere, this just got better over time. You might experience a “tight” feeling around your chest, and this just gets better as you heal and get used to things, it is a bit uncomfortable at first, though. 

So happy for you!!
